title: A Tiny Red Dot From the Baby Universe Might Be a Baby Black Hole
summary:
Picture the universe as a newborn, just 450 million years old, and imagine spotting a tiny, fiery-red speck shining in it. That is what the James Webb Space Telescope has done. The speck is called CW-LRD-z10, and astronomers think it might be one of the earliest black holes ever found. It could reveal how the biggest black holes began.

CW-LRD-z10 may belong to a mysterious family nicknamed "little red dots": small, extremely red objects packed into dense cocoons of gas. Many researchers think they are black holes pulling in gas and growing fast. If confirmed, this would be the earliest known example.

Scientists measured its redshift, which tells how far away it is: this one measured 10.36, meaning its light set out when the universe was only 450 million years old. The team found it in a 2025 search with Webb's mid-infrared instrument; it was the only candidate.

The clues fit like puzzle pieces. Its color is much redder in mid-infrared light than in near-infrared light, and its spectrum shows a "V-shaped" dip typical of little red dots, possible iron emission, and faint lines like those in other little red dots. No single clue proves the case alone, said study leader Takumi Tanaka, a doctoral student at the University of Tokyo. Together, though, they make a strong argument.

Still, scientists are being careful. The spectrum lacks the wide hydrogen lines that usually mark a little red dot, because that part was not covered in this study. Roberto Maiolino, a Cambridge professor not involved in the study, said it should only be considered a candidate for now, though the redshift looks reasonably solid. A closer galaxy is another possibility, but Tanaka said the data does not support it. The study was published on November 24 in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.
why_it_matters: If confirmed, CW-LRD-z10 would be the earliest known example of a little red dot, helping scientists work out how the biggest black holes in the universe began and grew so fast.

background_read: A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape it.
Astronomers study the early universe by looking at light that has traveled for a very long time, so the farther away an object is, the further back in time they are seeing.
The James Webb Space Telescope looks at infrared light, which lets it spot very distant and very red objects that other telescopes might miss.
'Little red dots' are a puzzling group of small, extremely red objects found in the early universe, and many scientists think they could be young black holes wrapped in gas.
